title: Lecture #41: Java Optional Explained from Scratch
topics: Getting values (get, isPresent, ifPresent, orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow, ifPresentOrElse)

questions.question: The notes call Optional a "mini stream". Which description best captures what an `Optional<T>` is?
options: A collection that can hold any number of T values, but at most one of them can be null
A subclass of T that adds null-safety to all of T's methods
A compile-time annotation telling the compiler that a variable may be null
A container object that holds either exactly one non-null value (present) or nothing (empty)
questions.explanation: An Optional wraps zero or one non-null value, while a Stream handles zero to many. It is an ordinary object (`private final T value`), not an annotation and not a subtype of T. Its value is either present or absent, never a stored null.

questions.question: In the lecture's Demo, `getName()` is changed to return `Optional.ofNullable(null)`. What does the program print?
questions.explanation: `ofNullable(null)` returns an empty Optional, so `ifPresentOrElse` runs the second argument (the empty-action) and prints "Unknown". The NPE option describes `Optional.of(null)`; `ofNullable` exists precisely to accept null.

questions.question: What does this program print?
questions.explanation: `map` turns `Optional["Ravi"]` into `Optional[4]`. `filter(len -> len > 4)` fails, so the Optional becomes empty and `orElse(-1)` returns -1. A filter that fails does not throw: it just turns the Optional empty, and the exception only happens if you call `get()` on that empty Optional.

questions.question: `findUser(id)` returns `Optional<User>`. Your endpoint must fail with an `IllegalArgumentException("No user " + id)` when the user is missing, and otherwise use the User. Which line is the cleanest correct choice?
options: `User u = findUser(id).orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("No user " + id));`
questions.explanation: `orElseThrow(Supplier)` returns the value if present and otherwise throws the exception you supply. `get()` also throws on an empty Optional, but it throws a generic `NoSuchElementException` without your message. `orElse(null)` brings back the very null problem Optional is meant to remove, and `ifPresent` returns void.

questions.question: In Demo2, `User` has a field `Optional<Address> address`. Why does the lecture write `user.flatMap(x -> x.address)` instead of `user.map(x -> x.address)` to get an `Optional<Address>`?
options: Because the function already returns an Optional; `map` would wrap it again, giving `Optional<Optional<Address>>`, while `flatMap` returns it as-is
Because `map` cannot access public fields, only getter methods
Because `flatMap` also checks that `address.city` is non-null
Because `map` throws `NullPointerException` when the user is empty, while `flatMap` does not
questions.explanation: `map(f)` puts f's result into a new Optional, so if f already returns `Optional<Address>`, you get a nested Optional. `flatMap` expects a function that returns an Optional and does not wrap again. Both methods handle an empty user safely by returning empty, so null-safety is not what separates them.

questions.question: `List<User> users`, where `u.getEmail()` returns `Optional<String>` (some users have no email). You need a `List<String>` of the emails that exist. Which pipeline from the lecture does this correctly?
questions.explanation: Mapping gives a `Stream<Optional<String>>`. Filtering on `isPresent()` keeps only non-empty Optionals, so the following `get()` is safe. Checking `x != null` is the tempting mistake: an empty Optional is not null, so it passes the filter and `get()` throws `NoSuchElementException`.

questions.question: You are refactoring the notes' "null-check hell" (`if (u != null) { if (u.getAddress() != null) { if (u.getAddress().getCity() != null) ... } }`). `getUser()` now returns `Optional<User>`, while `getAddress()` and `getCity()` still return plain values that may be null. Which chain prints the city only when every level is present?
questions.explanation: If the mapping function returns null, `map` produces an empty Optional, so a missing address or city stops the chain and `ifPresent` does nothing. `flatMap` does not compile here, because those getters return plain values, not Optionals. The `get()`-based versions bring back NPE or NoSuchElementException risks.

questions.question: What is the exact output?
questions.explanation: `orElse(fallback())` is a normal method argument, so `fallback()` runs (printing "fallback ") before `orElse` is even called, even though the value is present. `orElseGet` takes a Supplier and calls it only when the Optional is empty, so the second line prints just "Aditya". This is why expensive defaults belong in `orElseGet`.

questions.question: Which one of these expressions throws a `NullPointerException` when evaluated?
questions.explanation: `Optional.of(value)` requires a non-null value and throws NPE immediately for null. `ofNullable(null)` is empty, so `map` never calls the lambda. A `map` function that returns null simply produces an empty Optional. `orElse(null)` just returns null without throwing.

questions.question: `findEmail()` was changed to return `Optional<String>`, but one early-exit branch still says `return null;`. A caller does `findEmail().orElse("none")`. What happens when that branch runs, and what is the fix?
options: It throws `NullPointerException`, because the Optional reference itself is null; the branch must return `Optional.empty()`
It returns "none", because `orElse` treats a null Optional as empty
It fails to compile, because a method returning `Optional<String>` cannot contain `return null;`
It returns null, because `orElse` passes the null through
questions.explanation: Optional only protects you if the Optional object itself exists. Calling any method on a null reference throws NPE before `orElse` can run. `return null;` compiles for any reference return type, so the compiler will not catch this; a method returning Optional should never return null, so use `Optional.empty()`.
